prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I hold two fingers to my head, trigger my thumb, I say pow. I slice my throat with a single stroke, pull an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Remember the deaths we did together? Twiddling oven knobs in the air then thrusting our chins to inhale? I loved you so much during that experimental play when you slowly leant forward to nick your femoral artery then quietly bled out in your seat until curtain call, blood only we saw. As well as death, we’d mime marriage. I’d slide on a spectral ring and you’d shiver at the thrill of my thumb and fingertip sealing the deal for a second till the thought melted back into your skin. I am proficient at beginnings, the Air Year: the anniversary prior to paper for which ephemeral gifts are traditional. Only after our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear. Now the house is a mime scene. Mime blood all over the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, shirts, bras, dried to an airy crust under my nails. I slit my neck at the traffic lights, pow on the train, I suspend my non-knife above my head, “see what you’re making me do.” Red whirls rise from the cuts. All these huge thoughts come to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Remember, Twiddling, Air

outputs.L1:
I press two fingers to my head, pull the trigger with my thumb, and say, “Pow.” I slit my throat with a single stroke, drawing an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Remember the deaths we performed together? Twiddling imaginary oven knobs, then thrusting out our chins to inhale? I loved you so much during that experimental play, when you slowly leant forward to nick your femoral artery, then quietly bled out in your seat until curtain call—blood only we could see.

Alongside death, we mimed marriage. I would slip on a spectral ring, and you would shiver at the thrill of my thumb and fingertip sealing the deal for a second, until the thought melted back into your skin. I am proficient in beginnings: the Air Year, the anniversary before paper, for which ephemeral gifts are traditional. Only after our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear.

Now the house is a mime scene. Mime blood lies all over the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, shirts, bras; dried to an airy crust beneath my nails. I slit my neck at the traffic lights, say “Pow” on the train, suspend my non-knife above my head: “See what you’re making me do.” Red whorls rise from the cuts. All these immense thoughts come to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.
outputs.L2:
I press two fingertips against my temple, cock my thumb like a hammer, and whisper, bang. With one swift gesture, I cut across my neck; then I draw a nonexistent knife lengthwise over the vein. Do you recall all the ways we pretended to die together? Our hands would turn imaginary oven dials before we lifted our faces and breathed in the fictitious gas. I adored you fiercely in that experimental production, when you bent forward with deliberate slowness, opened your femoral artery, and silently emptied of blood in your chair until the final curtain—a hemorrhage visible to no one but us.

We acted out weddings, too. I would ease an insubstantial ring onto your finger, and you would tremble at the charge of my thumb and forefinger completing the ceremony, just for an instant, before the idea dissolved beneath your skin. I excel at first stages: the airy year, the anniversary that comes before paper, when tradition calls for gifts that cannot last. It was only when our rings took material form in silver that they vanished for good.

The house has since become a silent performance. Imaginary blood covers the floor, ground deep into the carpet, smeared across shirts and bras, and hardened beneath my fingernails into a weightless crust. At stoplights I open my throat; on the train I fire the make-believe gun. I raise my absent knife over my head and accuse you: “Look what you’ve driven me to.” Crimson spirals lift from every wound. Yet these enormous thoughts dissolve into emptiness. My shadow resembles the chalk border around a woman’s body, except she never leapt.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks back on a relationship in which mime once served as a private language between the lovers. Through gesture, they enacted imagined deaths, tenderness, and moments of intimacy, creating a world of shared possibility without making those experiences physically real. They even mimed a marriage, briefly performing the gestures of commitment before eventually exchanging genuine silver rings. Yet the moment their bond became tangible and formally defined, the closeness that had sustained it seemed to vanish. What had felt open and full of promise became fixed, and the relationship ultimately collapsed.

In the aftermath, the speaker is consumed by grief and repeatedly imagines dramatic acts of self-harm in ordinary, everyday settings. These violent fantasies reveal the intensity of her despair, but they remain imagined rather than enacted. Despite feeling emotionally overwhelmed and haunted by possible versions of her own death, she survives. She is left suspended between destruction and endurance, like “the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump”—marked by the shape of an imagined death, yet still unmistakably alive.
outputs.L4:
The speaker repeatedly reenacts the defining moments of a failed relationship through theatrical, wordless gestures. She mimes suicide, holding an imaginary gun to her head or imagining herself poised to jump, but the act remains only a performance. She also recalls the couple’s playful gestures toward marriage and intimacy, moments when they could pretend that love had already created a shared future. Later, the same imaginative space becomes filled with invisible wounds and blood, suggesting that the relationship’s end inflicted real emotional pain even though no physical injury can be seen.

These recurring gestures trace the movement of the relationship from hopeful play to devastating separation. What once seemed like a private game between lovers becomes a solitary ritual of grief. The speaker is haunted not only by what happened, but also by everything that might have happened: the marriage that never occurred, the life they never built, and the suicide she imagined but did not carry out. Her “huge thoughts” are therefore powerful precisely because they remain unrealized. They occupy her mind without becoming actions, leaving her suspended between memory, fantasy, and survival. Although loss continues to shape her identity, the final and most important fact is that she did not jump. Her refusal—or inability—to complete the imagined act becomes a quiet affirmation of endurance: she remains alive, wounded but present, defined as much by survival as by grief.
outputs.L5:
**Remember the Air**

Remember the summer evenings when we sat on the porch, twiddling blades of grass between our fingers as the daylight slowly faded. The air carried the scent of rain, warm earth, and distant flowers. We spoke of nothing important, yet every silence felt full.

Years later, I still return to that moment whenever life becomes too loud. I stop, breathe, and remember: not everything must be solved. Sometimes it is enough to sit quietly, twiddling a small thought between your fingers, and let the air carry the rest away.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a failed marriage, using mime, invisible weapons, imaginary deaths, and the traditional “paper anniversary” as recurring motifs.
counterfactuals.output:
**Paper Anniversary**

On our first anniversary, we gave each other paper. You folded yours into a white bird and placed it in my palm; I wrote *stay* on mine until the word became a small black door. Neither gift survived the evening. Your bird drowned in the kitchen sink. My door would not open.

After that, we became mimes of marriage. Each morning you lifted an invisible cup to your lips; I poured invisible coffee. We smiled through the glass wall we had built without bricks, pressing our hands to opposite sides. Guests admired our silence. They called it peace.

But the house was full of weapons no one could see. You carried a pistol shaped like a pause. I kept a knife made of remembering. At dinner, beneath the table, we drew them slowly. No blood appeared, only the napkins blooming between our fingers, white as surrender, thin as paper.

We died imaginary deaths for years. You fell whenever I said *always*. I vanished whenever you said *never*. Some nights I found you sprawled beside the bed, slain by a sentence I had not spoken. Some mornings you discovered my ghost brushing its teeth, rehearsing the gestures of a woman still alive.

Every anniversary returned us to paper: cards left unsigned, apologies folded into cranes, legal pads crowded with grievances. Paper covered the walls like pale ivy. Paper slept between us. Even our photographs seemed to rustle when we passed, as if the people inside were trying to escape.

At last, in the lawyer’s office, we performed our final mime. You pulled an invisible ring from your finger. I caught an invisible bullet in my chest. We both pretended not to die.

Then came the papers.

How softly they ended us—no blade, no gunshot, only our names traveling down separate lines. We signed where the small flags told us to sign. Outside, the wind lifted a scrap from the pavement and carried it briefly between us: a white bird, a torn vow, the last anniversary.

Neither of us reached for it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, surreal monologue in which a woman remembers how she and her former lover used to pantomime suicide and marriage, only to find that the relationship vanished once their wedding rings became real.
counterfactuals.output:
We used to rehearse our deaths in the kitchen.

You would hold the bread knife to your wrist—backward, harmless—and sigh like a silent-film prince. I would knot the curtain around my throat and stand on a chair, one hand pressed to my brow, waiting for you to notice. We were very young, or else already ghosts. It is difficult now to tell the difference.

Sometimes we died together. Gas from an unlit stove. A leap from the blue rug, which became, by agreement, a cliff above a black and patient sea. Afterward we would lie side by side on the linoleum, suppressing laughter, our fingers almost touching.

Then one of us would resurrect and propose.

You made rings from orange peel, from wire, from the silver paper around chewing gum. I made veils from dish towels. The broom stood in for a priest. The cupboards watched with their many square, wooden eyes.

Do you take this woman?

I do, you whispered.

Until death?

Especially after.

We believed love required costumes. A little blood painted at the mouth. A bouquet of dead matches. We married each other a hundred times and killed ourselves a hundred more. Each ceremony erased the last. Each death left us ravenous. At midnight we ate jam from the jar and swore we would never become ordinary.

Then came the real room with the real clerk. The real flowers bruising in their vase. Your mother crying honestly. My father wearing a suit that smelled of rain.

And the rings.

How bright they were—two small, perfect verdicts.

You slid mine onto my finger, and something in the world went quiet. Not the reverent quiet people speak of, but the quiet after a bird strikes a window. I looked at you and saw no groom, no lover, no boy dying beautifully on the kitchen floor. Only a man fastening a lock.

Perhaps you saw the same in me.

We went home married, and found the apartment empty, though all our furniture remained. Our shadows no longer met in the hallway. The broom had forgotten its holy office. The blue rug was only a rug. Even the knives seemed embarrassed by their blunt old roles.

We tried again.

You lay on the floor and clutched your chest. I waited for laughter, but none came. I wrapped myself in the curtain, and you asked whether I meant to wash it. We stood before the cupboards and repeated our vows, but the words fell between us like teeth.

The gold had made everything literal.

That was the cruelty of it. We had survived every imaginary death, but we could not survive an actual marriage. The moment the rings became real, we became imaginary.

Soon you began vanishing in pieces. First your voice from the bedroom. Then your face from photographs. Then the weight of you from your side of the bed. One morning your ring lay on the table, a tiny sun with no planet left to burn.

People ask when you left.

I tell them I don’t remember.

But I do.

You left at the altar, just after you said yes. So did I. Two strangers wore our bodies home, and they lived together for a while, politely, listening at night for the laughter of the dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an experimental flash-fiction passage exploring heartbreak and self-destructive thoughts through extended metaphors of air, performance, spectral objects, and a house staged like a mime scene.
counterfactuals.output:
After you left, the air kept rehearsing you.

It entered through the cracked window in your old costume—cold at the wrists, smelling faintly of rain—and bowed to the empty chair. Every evening it performed the same scene: the curtain breathing, the lamp trembling, the glass on the table applauding with one small ring.

The house had become a mime’s house. I pulled invisible doors from invisible walls. I leaned against rooms that were no longer there. In the kitchen, I lifted a phantom cup to my lips and drank what the audience understood to be poison, though it was only silence, though silence can be prepared many ways.

Your belongings grew spectral after midnight. The coat floated without a body. The keys unlocked nothing and still turned. A pale shoe waited under the bed like a severed moon. I began speaking to these objects in stage whispers.

*Tell me how to disappear.*

They answered by passing through me.

Some nights, my thoughts stood in the balcony and shouted for an encore. Break the glass. Step into the dark. Stop breathing and call it a final act. But the body, poor understudy, kept forgetting to die. It inhaled on cue. It stumbled into morning wearing my face.

So I painted a door on the wall.

For weeks I practiced opening it.

On the last night, the house held its breath. The furniture took its marks. Your ghost sat in the front row, beautiful and bored. I placed my hand on the painted knob and felt—impossibly—a draft.

Not an exit.

Air.

Real air, unscripted, slipping through the plaster.

I pressed my mouth to the wall and breathed until the scene collapsed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in a contemporary literary style about the aftermath of divorce. Contrast playful gestures of pretend death and pretend marriage with solid silver rings, then end with the image of the narrator’s shadow as the chalk outline of someone who did not jump.
counterfactuals.output:
After the divorce, I became superstitious about objects.

The blue mug was the mug I had bought the week he left. The fern was the fern that survived our final argument, though neither of us remembered to water it for a month. In the cutlery drawer, forks we had chosen together lay beside spoons from my childhood, and every morning I had to decide which history to stir into my coffee.

Our daughter, six, treated the separation as a problem of staging.

“Pretend you’re dead,” she said, aiming two fingers at me across the living-room rug.

I fell extravagantly, knocking a cushion to the floor. She shrieked with delight and climbed onto my chest to inspect the body.

“Now wake up.”

I opened my eyes.

“You were only pretend dead,” she explained.

This was how she liked her catastrophes: brief, reversible, under her command. Sometimes she died instead, collapsing in the hallway with her tongue out, and I had to revive her with the magic password, which changed daily. Pancakes. Rhinoceros. Daddy’s new apartment.

Other afternoons, she married us again.

She tore strips from the supermarket receipts and wrapped them around our fingers. She stood on the ottoman and made us promise things.

“Promise to share.”

We promised.

“Promise not to shout.”

We promised.

“Promise to live in the same house forever.”

Her father looked at me. I looked at the paper ring loosening around my knuckle, already going soft with sweat.

“We promise to love you forever,” I said.

She considered the substitution, then pronounced us married.

The real rings were in a velvet box at the back of my dresser. Solid silver, slightly scratched, heavier than they looked. Mine still held the small oval dent from the night I shut my hand in the kitchen drawer and laughed until I cried. His had been engraved inside with a date we no longer celebrated. For years, their weight had seemed proof: metal against skin, continuity made visible. But permanence is only a quality of matter. Silver persists. People alter.

When we divided the house, neither of us knew what to do with them.

“Sell them?” he said.

“For what?”

He shrugged. A dinner, perhaps. Half a month of groceries. Two train tickets in opposite directions.

So I kept them. Not from hope, I told myself, but because throwing them away would have been another ceremony, and we had exhausted our appetite for ceremonies. The courthouse had given us a stamped decree. The bank had separated our money with a few clicks. Friends had learned to invite us on alternating weekends. Even grief became administrative: new passwords, new emergency contacts, his name removed from the dentist’s file.

At night, after our daughter was asleep, I sometimes put both rings in my palm. They looked like coins from a country that had ceased to exist. I liked their coldness. I liked that they did not pretend. They did not die and rise again. They did not marry anyone. They were merely solid silver, faithful only to their own shape.

By spring, the paper rings had vanished into bins, pockets, the mouths of vacuum cleaners. The fern put out one pale leaf. I learned to cook for one and a half. He learned to braid our daughter’s hair. We became courteous in doorways.

One evening, walking home alone, I crossed the bridge where the river held the last light in broken pieces. Below me, the water kept moving without arrival or apology. Cars passed, each carrying a life I could not imagine. I stood at the railing until the lamps came on behind me, and there on the pavement my shadow stretched long and still: the chalk outline of someone who did not jump.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a disturbing first-person prose poem where grand gestures of despair—finger guns, invisible knives, imaginary blood—repeatedly “come to nothing,” suggesting both emotional crisis and survival.
counterfactuals.output:
Every morning I press two fingers to my temple and rehearse the small theater of thunder. My thumb falls. The room does not flinch. No smoke loosens from my hair, no red weather stains the wall. The grand gesture comes to nothing, as grand gestures often do, and I am left holding the ridiculous little animal of my hand.

At noon I find an invisible knife among the dishes. It has no handle, no edge, yet I carry it carefully. I draw it across the hours. I cut the day in half, then quarters, then pieces small enough to swallow without chewing. The knife comes to nothing. The hours leak no blood. They only continue, pale and stubborn, beneath my touch.

By evening I am drenched in imaginary blood. It pours from the secret trapdoors of me, slicks the floorboards, fills my shoes, rises to my mouth with its warm metallic hymn. I wade from room to room, leaving no footprints. I touch the mirror and my fingers come away clean. Even the blood comes to nothing.

This is how despair embarrasses me: with its velvet curtains, its orchestral dark, its insistence that something enormous is about to happen. I wait for the chandelier to fall. I wait for the house to open its black mouth. I wait for my body to become an abandoned address.

Nothing happens.

The kettle begins its thin scream. A truck groans past. Somewhere inside the wall, a pipe knocks like a trapped heart asking to be let out. I make tea with the hands that failed to become weapons. I drink it with the mouth that failed to become a wound.

At midnight I lie down beside all my vanished catastrophes. They crowd the bed: the unloaded finger guns, the blunt invisible knives, the blood that never was. They whisper that tomorrow they will be magnificent. Tomorrow they will mean it.

But morning keeps coming to nothing, too—first gray, then silver, then ordinary gold. And I keep coming with it: unshot, uncut, unstained, terribly alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
